VIDEO.title: Matthew 10:16-33 – The Holy Spirit Will Speak Through the Disciples?
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 10:16-33, the middle of Jesus' mission discourse. He sends the Twelve as sheep among wolves, warns of courts, floggings, governors and kings, tells them not to worry about what to say, and repeats 'do not fear,' ending with a promise and a warning: whoever confesses Him He will confess before His Father.

From verse 17 on, Jesus seems to look past this first trip (only to Israel, 10:5) to a later time of persecution, when they stand before governors and Gentiles, as in Acts. Some scholars think Matthew gathered sayings by theme; either way, Jesus is preparing them for when He is not physically with them.

Who are the wolves? Jesus called the crowds sheep without a shepherd (9:36), echoing Ezekiel 34's bad shepherds, and warned of false prophets who are 'inwardly are ravenous wolves' (7:15). Zephaniah 3 calls Jerusalem's judges 'wolves at evening.' The wolves are the leaders who should have known the Tanakh and recognized their Messiah.

'The Spirit of your Father who speaks in you' (10:20): hear it as a Jew would. The ruach of God hovers at creation, and Ezekiel 36-37 promise God's Spirit within His people to cause them to walk in His statutes, and to breathe life into dry bones. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, where He answered every test with 'It is written.'

So the Spirit is not a 'good possession' that turns disciples into megaphones. He brings to mind God's word. That is what Acts shows: Peter at Pentecost, Stephen's speech, Paul and Silas speaking 'the word of the Lord' to the jailer.

The lesson for the disciples, then and now: when the disciples of Jesus know God's word, they'll never fear to know what to say. The answer to anxiety about being caught unprepared is to know God's word even more.
QUOTES: It's the persecutors who should dread God.
To acknowledge him is to declare allegiance to him, is to declare solidarity with Jesus.
Jesus is saying that in the moment of trouble, the Holy Spirit will guide the disciples to speak the word of God.
When the disciples of Jesus know God's word, they'll never fear to know what to say.
The practice of thinking through the perspective of the original audience, it's really like a muscle that gets stronger over time.

method.h: Find the lesson for the original audience
method.p: The teacher talks through his method out loud: (1) Who is the original audience? The disciples. (2) Why is Jesus speaking to them this way? (3) What did they need to know that they did not? Verse 19 says 'do not worry,' so they would face anxiety. Put the pieces together (anxiety, the Spirit, God's word) and a lesson appears. It is a muscle that grows with practice.

LSB_QUOTES.text: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.
I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you will be careful to do My judgments.
So do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows.

WOLVES.title: Shrewd as serpents, innocent as doves

src.text: “Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves.

lines.text: Jesus tells them to be both wise and innocent with those who will respond with hostility, then warns of physical harm and repeats: do not fear. Their experience will mirror His.
This is not the first mention of sheep: the crowds were 'like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36), a callback to Ezekiel 34.

left.text: ‘Thus says Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will seek My flock from their hand and make them cease from shepherding the flock.

right.text: Her princes in her midst are roaring lions; / Her judges are wolves at evening; / They leave nothing to gnaw for the morning.

lines.text: In Jesus' day it got worse: the shepherds pretended to be sheep but were wolves inside. 'Beware of the false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves' (7:15).
The wolves are the leaders, officials and priests: those who should have known the Tanakh and recognized their Messiah, yet persecuted God's messengers in the name of righteousness.

src.text: But beware of men, for they will deliver you over to the courts and flog you in their synagogues; and you will even be brought before governors and kings for My sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.

lines.text: In 10:5 He said 'Do not go in the way of the Gentiles'; now they will testify to Gentiles. Jesus is looking beyond this first mission to the persecution of Acts, when the people's favor had faded.
Synagogue flogging was a judicial penalty for members, so Jesus pictures His followers still inside the synagogues, as in Acts.
Paul: 'Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one' (2 Corinthians 11:24). The apostles were beaten by the Sanhedrin and left 'rejoicing' (Acts 5:40-41).

WOLVES.title: Until the Son of Man comes

src.text: “But whenever they persecute you in this city, flee to the next; for truly I say to you, you will not finish going through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes.

lines.text: This verse has perplexed Christians for a long time. The teacher suspects it is Jesus coming in judgment on Israel and its temple in AD 70: the explanation with the fewest problems, he says, though he leaves the topic for another time.
Other readings: the resurrection, Pentecost, or His final return, with the mission to Israel still unfinished until then. See Debates below.

RUACH.title: Do not worry about what to say

src.text: But when they deliver you over, do not worry about how or what you are to say; for it will be given to you in that hour what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

lines.text: Hear it as a Jew who grew up in the Tanakh would. The Spirit (ruach) is there at creation, 'hovering over the surface of the waters' (Genesis 1:2), and at the moments God saves His people.
Matthew does not mention the Holy Spirit often; when he does, it is often tied to the spread of God's kingdom.

src.text: Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you will be careful to do My judgments.

lines.text: God promises to gather His people, sprinkle clean water on them, and put His Spirit within them. Notice what the Spirit does: He causes them to walk in God's statutes and obey Him.
Peter at Pentecost: 'I will pour out My Spirit on all mankind' (Acts 2:17, from Joel 2:28).

src.text: “And My servant David will be king over them, and they will all have one shepherd; and they will walk in My judgments and keep My statutes and do them.

lines.text: The next chapter: a valley of dry bones, and the prophet calls the breath to come and give them life. The promises end with one shepherd, David's heir, and the same phrase: they will walk in My judgments.
The Hebrew ruach is 'breath,' 'wind' and 'Spirit' in the same chapter (37:9, 14).

left.text: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.

right.text: But He answered and said, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.’”

lines.text: The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, and every time He answered the devil with Scripture. The video connects it to Ezekiel 36-37: the Spirit causes God's people to walk by His word.

So 10:20 is no magic trick or 'good possession' that turns people into megaphones for novel sayings. In trouble, the Spirit guides disciples to speak the word of God, which they know from the Tanakh and from Jesus' teaching.

That is what Acts shows: Peter's Pentecost sermon, Stephen recounting Israel's story, and Paul and Silas: 'they spoke the word of the Lord to him together with all who were in his household' (Acts 16:32).

src.text: It is enough for the disciple that he become like his teacher, and the slave like his master. If they have called the head of the house Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household! “Therefore do not fear them, for there is nothing concealed that will not be revealed, and hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in your ear, proclaim upon the housetops.

lines.text: 'Whispered in your ear… proclaim upon the housetops' is an idiom: what Jesus tells them privately now, they must speak publicly later.
The Pharisees had already said He cast out demons by 'the ruler of the demons' (9:34); in 12:24 they name Beelzebul. The captions spell it 'be ela bull.'

src.text: Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? And yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows.

lines.text: 'Fear' comes three times in verses 28-31. Jesus is not trying to make His people afraid of the Father; then 'do not fear' (10:31) would make no sense. He assures them that those who kill the body are not as powerful as the One who can destroy soul and body in hell.
So it is not the apostles, doing the Father's will, who should dread God this way. It's the persecutors.
An assarion was a small Roman copper coin. Luke has five sparrows for two (Luke 12:6-7).

src.text: “Therefore everyone who confesses Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father who is in heaven.

lines.text: To confess (acknowledge) Jesus is to declare allegiance and solidarity with Him, even in persecution and suffering. Jesus will declare the same of us before His Father; deny Him, and He will do the same.
The teacher says this promise, more than the warning about hell, is the one that should give us pause.
Peter later denies Him three times (26:69-75), and is restored (John 21:15-19).

TERMS.def: Hebrew for breath, wind or spirit; the Spirit of God (Genesis 1:2; Ezekiel 36:27; 37:9, 14).
Matthew's phrase in 10:20 for the Holy Spirit; Mark 13:11 says 'the Holy Spirit.'
A judicial beating given to members by synagogue courts; Deuteronomy 25:3 limits it to forty lashes.
A name for the ruler of the demons (12:24); the leaders used it to slander Jesus.
Flat roofs where people talked and announcements were made: 'proclaim upon the housetops' means say it publicly.
The place of final judgment (10:28); named for the Valley of Hinnom.
A small Roman copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius; the KJV 'farthing.'
A 'hint' that recalls a larger Old Testament passage. The captions hear it as 'Rome.'

WORDS.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Look up: BDAG, πνεῦμα.
To confess, acknowledge, declare openly. Look up: BDAG, ὁμολογέω.
Breath, wind, spirit; the Spirit of God. Look up: BDB or HALOT, רוּחַ.

BACKGROUND.p: Synagogues served as local courts as well as places of prayer. Deuteronomy 25:2-3 allowed up to forty lashes; the custom of 'forty less one' kept the limit from being broken (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Judea was ruled by Roman governors from Caesarea (Pilate, later Felix and Festus), while Herod's family ruled as kings or tetrarchs (Antipas in Galilee; Agrippa I and II). Acts shows apostles before each.
Sparrows were among the cheapest food sold in markets. Jesus' point: if God tracks even these, He knows every hair on His disciples' heads.

The same Hebrew word covers breath, wind and spirit. The Spirit gives life (Genesis 2:7 uses another word, neshamah, for breath; Ezekiel 37 uses ruach) and empowers prophets to speak God's word (Numbers 11:25; 2 Samuel 23:2).

DEBATES.h: When does the Son of Man come (10:23)?
DEBATES.p: The video: in judgment on Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70. Others: the resurrection, Pentecost, or the final return, with the mission to Israel unfinished until then. Chrysostom took it of the troubles before the cross: Jesus would rejoin them before they had gone round Palestine. It remains one of Matthew's hardest verses.

DEBATES.h: Does the Spirit give new words?
DEBATES.p: The video: the Spirit brings to mind God's word that disciples already know (John 14:26). Chrysostom: it raises them 'unto the dignity of the prophets.' Both agree the help is real and comes 'in that hour.'

Some scholars think Matthew gathered Jesus' sayings by theme, since Mark and Luke place similar words in His last week (Mark 13:9-13; Luke 21:12-19). Others think Jesus repeated such warnings. Either way, 10:17-23 looks beyond the first mission.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: In Zephaniah 3:3-4 the judges are the 'wolves at evening'; the princes are lions, the prophets 'reckless, treacherous men,' and the priests profane the sanctuary. The video groups them all as wolves.
The link between Matthew 7:15 and Zephaniah 3 is the video's reading; Jesus does not cite Zephaniah there.
The synagogue-flogging point is attributed to D. A. Carson; the wording could not be checked here, so read his commentary before quoting it.
Matthew's Spirit verses are not all about spreading the kingdom: several are about Jesus' conception and baptism (1:18, 20; 3:16).

The closing preview says John the Baptist's disciples come next; the next video is Matthew 10:34-42 ('not peace, but a sword'). John's question comes in 11:2-6. The captions also hear 'remez' as 'Rome.'

QUESTIONS: When have you felt like a sheep among wolves? What would 'shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves' have looked like?
How does hearing 'Spirit' as ruach, through Ezekiel 36-37, change how you read 10:20?
Which do you find harder: not fearing people, or confessing Jesus before them?
What does the image of sparrows and numbered hairs say about how God sees you?
Practice the teacher's method: who is the audience, why is Jesus speaking this way, and what did they need to know?
What part of God's word could you get to know better this week, so you are ready when asked?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The teacher talks through how he finds a lesson. The original audience is the disciples listening to their rabbi. Why is Jesus speaking this way? He is preparing them to go out, and for a time when He will not be physically present. In verse 19 He says 'do not worry,' so they either struggle with anxiety now or will when these things happen. Put that together with the ruach of God from Ezekiel 36 and 37, who causes God's people to walk in His statutes and brings them back to what the Lord has said, and with John 14:26, where the Holy Spirit brings to remembrance all that Jesus said. The lesson: when the disciples of Jesus know God's word, they'll never fear to know what to say. This is not a free pass to skip reading Scripture; it depends on how well we know God's word. The same is true today: the answer to anxiety about being caught off guard by skeptics is to know God's word even more.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): choose one passage you would want to have ready if someone asked about your faith (for example Psalm 2, Isaiah 53 or Ezekiel 36:26-27). Read it daily this week and say it aloud once from memory by Sunday.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 10:16-33, the middle of Jesus' mission discourse. He sends the Twelve as sheep among wolves, warns of courts, floggings, governors and kings, tells them not to worry about what to say, and repeats 'do not fear,' ending with a promise and a warning: whoever confesses Him He will confess before His Father.
- From verse 17 on, Jesus seems to look past this first trip (only to Israel, 10:5) to a later time of persecution, when they stand before governors and Gentiles, as in Acts. Some scholars think Matthew gathered sayings by theme; either way, Jesus is preparing them for when He is not physically with them.
- Who are the wolves? Jesus called the crowds sheep without a shepherd (9:36), echoing Ezekiel 34's bad shepherds, and warned of false prophets who are 'inwardly are ravenous wolves' (7:15). Zephaniah 3 calls Jerusalem's judges 'wolves at evening.' The wolves are the leaders who should have known the Tanakh and recognized their Messiah.
- 'The Spirit of your Father who speaks in you' (10:20): hear it as a Jew would. The ruach of God hovers at creation, and Ezekiel 36-37 promise God's Spirit within His people to cause them to walk in His statutes, and to breathe life into dry bones. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, where He answered every test with 'It is written.'
- So the Spirit is not a 'good possession' that turns disciples into megaphones. He brings to mind God's word. That is what Acts shows: Peter at Pentecost, Stephen's speech, Paul and Silas speaking 'the word of the Lord' to the jailer.
- The lesson for the disciples, then and now: when the disciples of Jesus know God's word, they'll never fear to know what to say. The answer to anxiety about being caught unprepared is to know God's word even more.

### Find the lesson for the original audience
The teacher talks through his method out loud: (1) Who is the original audience? The disciples. (2) Why is Jesus speaking to them this way? (3) What did they need to know that they did not? Verse 19 says 'do not worry,' so they would face anxiety. Put the pieces together (anxiety, the Spirit, God's word) and a lesson appears. It is a muscle that grows with practice.

   (video) Jesus tells them to be both wise and innocent with those who will respond with hostility, then warns of physical harm and repeats: do not fear. Their experience will mirror His.
   (video) This is not the first mention of sheep: the crowds were 'like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36), a callback to Ezekiel 34. (Matthew 9:36)
2. Who are the wolves?: Shepherds who fed themselves
   Ezekiel (Ezekiel 34:10, LSB): "‘Thus says Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will seek My flock from their hand and make them cease from shepherding the flock."
   Zephaniah (Zephaniah 3:3, LSB): "Her princes in her midst are roaring lions; / Her judges are wolves at evening; / They leave nothing to gnaw for the morning."
   (video) In Jesus' day it got worse: the shepherds pretended to be sheep but were wolves inside. 'Beware of the false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves' (7:15). (Matthew 7:15)
   (video) The wolves are the leaders, officials and priests: those who should have known the Tanakh and recognized their Messiah, yet persecuted God's messengers in the name of righteousness. (John 16:2-3)
3. Courts and synagogues · Matthew 10:17-18: Before governors and kings
   Witness Matthew 10:17-18: "But beware of men, for they will deliver you over to the courts and flog you in their synagogues; and you will even be brought before governors and kings for My sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:17-18
   (video) In 10:5 He said 'Do not go in the way of the Gentiles'; now they will testify to Gentiles. Jesus is looking beyond this first mission to the persecution of Acts, when the people's favor had faded.
   (video) Synagogue flogging was a judicial penalty for members, so Jesus pictures His followers still inside the synagogues, as in Acts. (Acts 22:19)
   [Background] Paul: 'Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one' (2 Corinthians 11:24). The apostles were beaten by the Sanhedrin and left 'rejoicing' (Acts 5:40-41). (2 Corinthians 11:24; Acts 5:40-41)
4. Verse 23: Until the Son of Man comes
   Puzzle Matthew 10:23: "“But whenever they persecute you in this city, flee to the next; for truly I say to you, you will not finish going through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:23
   (video) This verse has perplexed Christians for a long time. The teacher suspects it is Jesus coming in judgment on Israel and its temple in AD 70: the explanation with the fewest problems, he says, though he leaves the topic for another time.
   [Background] Other readings: the resurrection, Pentecost, or His final return, with the mission to Israel still unfinished until then. See Debates below.

## The Spirit of your Father
1. Matthew 10:19-20: Do not worry about what to say
   Spirit Matthew 10:19-20: "But when they deliver you over, do not worry about how or what you are to say; for it will be given to you in that hour what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:19-20
   (video) Hear it as a Jew who grew up in the Tanakh would. The Spirit (ruach) is there at creation, 'hovering over the surface of the waters' (Genesis 1:2), and at the moments God saves His people. (Genesis 1:2)
   (video) Matthew does not mention the Holy Spirit often; when he does, it is often tied to the spread of God's kingdom. (Matthew 12:28; Matthew 28:19)
2. Ezekiel 36:25-27: My Spirit within you
   New heart Ezekiel 36:26-27: "Moreover, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes, and you will be careful to do My judgments." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Ezekiel+36:26-27
   (video) God promises to gather His people, sprinkle clean water on them, and put His Spirit within them. Notice what the Spirit does: He causes them to walk in God's statutes and obey Him.
   [Background] Peter at Pentecost: 'I will pour out My Spirit on all mankind' (Acts 2:17, from Joel 2:28). (Acts 2:16-17)
3. Ezekiel 37: Breath into dry bones
   Life Ezekiel 37:24: "“And My servant David will be king over them, and they will all have one shepherd; and they will walk in My judgments and keep My statutes and do them." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Ezekiel+37:24
   (video) The next chapter: a valley of dry bones, and the prophet calls the breath to come and give them life. The promises end with one shepherd, David's heir, and the same phrase: they will walk in My judgments. (Ezekiel 37:9-10)
   [Background] The Hebrew ruach is 'breath,' 'wind' and 'Spirit' in the same chapter (37:9, 14). (Ezekiel 37:14)
4. Matthew 4:1-4 and Acts: It is written
   Matthew (Matthew 4:1, LSB): "Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil."
   Jesus (Matthew 4:4, LSB): "But He answered and said, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.’”"
   (video) The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, and every time He answered the devil with Scripture. The video connects it to Ezekiel 36-37: the Spirit causes God's people to walk by His word.
   (video) So 10:20 is no magic trick or 'good possession' that turns people into megaphones for novel sayings. In trouble, the Spirit guides disciples to speak the word of God, which they know from the Tanakh and from Jesus' teaching.
   (video) That is what Acts shows: Peter's Pentecost sermon, Stephen recounting Israel's story, and Paul and Silas: 'they spoke the word of the Lord to him together with all who were in his household' (Acts 16:32). (Acts 2:14-36; Acts 7:2-53; Acts 16:30-32)

## Do not fear
1. Matthew 10:24-27: Proclaim it on the housetops
   Speak up Matthew 10:25-27: "It is enough for the disciple that he become like his teacher, and the slave like his master. If they have called the head of the house Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household! “Therefore do not fear them, for there is nothing concealed that will not be revealed, and hidden that will not be known. What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in your ear, proclaim upon the housetops." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:25-27
   (video) 'Whispered in your ear… proclaim upon the housetops' is an idiom: what Jesus tells them privately now, they must speak publicly later.
   [Background] The Pharisees had already said He cast out demons by 'the ruler of the demons' (9:34); in 12:24 they name Beelzebul. The captions spell it 'be ela bull.' (Matthew 9:34; Matthew 12:24)
2. Matthew 10:28-31: More valuable than many sparrows
   Fear not Matthew 10:29-31: "Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? And yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:29-31
   (video) 'Fear' comes three times in verses 28-31. Jesus is not trying to make His people afraid of the Father; then 'do not fear' (10:31) would make no sense. He assures them that those who kill the body are not as powerful as the One who can destroy soul and body in hell.
   (video) So it is not the apostles, doing the Father's will, who should dread God this way. It's the persecutors.
   [Background] An assarion was a small Roman copper coin. Luke has five sparrows for two (Luke 12:6-7). (Luke 12:6-7)
3. Matthew 10:32-33: Confess Me before men
   Allegiance Matthew 10:32-33: "“Therefore everyone who confesses Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father who is in heaven." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+10:32-33
   (video) To confess (acknowledge) Jesus is to declare allegiance and solidarity with Him, even in persecution and suffering. Jesus will declare the same of us before His Father; deny Him, and He will do the same.
   (video) The teacher says this promise, more than the warning about hell, is the one that should give us pause.
   [Background] Peter later denies Him three times (26:69-75), and is restored (John 21:15-19). (Matthew 26:69-75; John 21:15-19)

## Key people
- Jesus: Prepares the Twelve for persecution, promises the Spirit's help, and calls them not to fear. [Background] Mark 13:9-13 and Luke 21:12-19 place similar words in His last week.
- The Twelve: Sheep sent among wolves; anxious, and told not to be. [Background] In Acts they are flogged, jailed and brought before rulers (Acts 4-5).
- The wolves: The leaders, officials and priests who should have known the Tanakh. [Background] Jesus says they will flog His messengers in their synagogues (23:34).
- Governors and kings: Where the disciples will testify before Gentiles. [Background] Paul stood before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa at Caesarea (Acts 24-26).
- Ezekiel: Promised God's Spirit within His people and saw breath enter dry bones. [Background] A priest-prophet among the exiles in Babylon (Ezekiel 1:1-3).
- Stephen: Answered his accusers by recounting God's word. [Background] He was 'full of the Holy Spirit' as he died (Acts 7:55).
- Paul and Silas: Spoke the word of the Lord to the Philippian jailer. [Background] They had been beaten with rods and jailed (Acts 16:22-24).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: A synagogue town: 'flog you in their synagogues' (10:17).
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas's capital: a 'king' of the kind 10:18 describes.
- Jerusalem (named in the video): Seat of the Sanhedrin, where the apostles were beaten (Acts 5:40), and Stephen was stoned.
- Caesarea Maritima: The Roman governors' seat, where Paul testified before Felix, Festus and Agrippa (Acts 24-26).

## Key terms
- Ruach: Hebrew for breath, wind or spirit; the Spirit of God (Genesis 1:2; Ezekiel 36:27; 37:9, 14).
- Spirit of your Father: Matthew's phrase in 10:20 for the Holy Spirit; Mark 13:11 says 'the Holy Spirit.'
- Synagogue flogging: A judicial beating given to members by synagogue courts; Deuteronomy 25:3 limits it to forty lashes.
- Beelzebul: A name for the ruler of the demons (12:24); the leaders used it to slander Jesus.
- Housetops: Flat roofs where people talked and announcements were made: 'proclaim upon the housetops' means say it publicly.
- Hell (Gehenna): The place of final judgment (10:28); named for the Valley of Hinnom. [Background]
- Assarion: A small Roman copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius; the KJV 'farthing.' [Background]
- Remez: A 'hint' that recalls a larger Old Testament passage. The captions hear it as 'Rome.'

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Synagogue discipline: Synagogues served as local courts as well as places of prayer. Deuteronomy 25:2-3 allowed up to forty lashes; the custom of 'forty less one' kept the limit from being broken (2 Corinthians 11:24).
- Governors and kings: Judea was ruled by Roman governors from Caesarea (Pilate, later Felix and Festus), while Herod's family ruled as kings or tetrarchs (Antipas in Galilee; Agrippa I and II). Acts shows apostles before each.
- Sparrows in the market: Sparrows were among the cheapest food sold in markets. Jesus' point: if God tracks even these, He knows every hair on His disciples' heads.
- Ruach in the Old Testament: The same Hebrew word covers breath, wind and spirit. The Spirit gives life (Genesis 2:7 uses another word, neshamah, for breath; Ezekiel 37 uses ruach) and empowers prophets to speak God's word (Numbers 11:25; 2 Samuel 23:2).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- When does the Son of Man come (10:23)? The video: in judgment on Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70. Others: the resurrection, Pentecost, or the final return, with the mission to Israel unfinished until then. Chrysostom took it of the troubles before the cross: Jesus would rejoin them before they had gone round Palestine. It remains one of Matthew's hardest verses.
- Does the Spirit give new words? The video: the Spirit brings to mind God's word that disciples already know (John 14:26). Chrysostom: it raises them 'unto the dignity of the prophets.' Both agree the help is real and comes 'in that hour.'
- One speech or gathered sayings? Some scholars think Matthew gathered Jesus' sayings by theme, since Mark and Luke place similar words in His last week (Mark 13:9-13; Luke 21:12-19). Others think Jesus repeated such warnings. Either way, 10:17-23 looks beyond the first mission.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- In Zephaniah 3:3-4 the judges are the 'wolves at evening'; the princes are lions, the prophets 'reckless, treacherous men,' and the priests profane the sanctuary. The video groups them all as wolves.
- The link between Matthew 7:15 and Zephaniah 3 is the video's reading; Jesus does not cite Zephaniah there.
- The synagogue-flogging point is attributed to D. A. Carson; the wording could not be checked here, so read his commentary before quoting it.
- Matthew's Spirit verses are not all about spreading the kingdom: several are about Jesus' conception and baptism (1:18, 20; 3:16).
- The closing preview says John the Baptist's disciples come next; the next video is Matthew 10:34-42 ('not peace, but a sword'). John's question comes in 11:2-6. The captions also hear 'remez' as 'Rome.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. When have you felt like a sheep among wolves? What would 'shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves' have looked like?
2. How does hearing 'Spirit' as ruach, through Ezekiel 36-37, change how you read 10:20?
3. Which do you find harder: not fearing people, or confessing Jesus before them?
4. What does the image of sparrows and numbered hairs say about how God sees you?
5. Practice the teacher's method: who is the audience, why is Jesus speaking this way, and what did they need to know?
6. What part of God's word could you get to know better this week, so you are ready when asked?

## Application
- (video) The teacher talks through how he finds a lesson. The original audience is the disciples listening to their rabbi. Why is Jesus speaking this way? He is preparing them to go out, and for a time when He will not be physically present. In verse 19 He says 'do not worry,' so they either struggle with anxiety now or will when these things happen. Put that together with the ruach of God from Ezekiel 36 and 37, who causes God's people to walk in His statutes and brings them back to what the Lord has said, and with John 14:26, where the Holy Spirit brings to remembrance all that Jesus said. The lesson: when the disciples of Jesus know God's word, they'll never fear to know what to say. This is not a free pass to skip reading Scripture; it depends on how well we know God's word. The same is true today: the answer to anxiety about being caught off guard by skeptics is to know God's word even more.
- Study note (added): choose one passage you would want to have ready if someone asked about your faith (for example Psalm 2, Isaiah 53 or Ezekiel 36:26-27). Read it daily this week and say it aloud once from memory by Sunday.
